title: Year two close: his own words
hookLine: the truths, the path, the middle-length, the long, the short, the connected, the numbered

lines: A YEAR OF HIS OWN WORDS.
cards: A year ago, year two opened with a promise: the Buddha's own words. Not stories about him. Not commentary.
The discourses themselves, as the early collections keep them. Some days it was a single line. Some days it was a long walk through a long sutta.
Today, from the lookout, one line from each stretch of the road.

teach.b: First, the four noble truths, from the first sermon at the Deer Park: there is suffering; it has a cause, which is craving; it can end; and there's a way.

Then the eightfold path, factor by factor, six days each: view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration. The line to keep: the middle way, between chasing pleasure and punishing yourself.
Then the Middle-Length Sayings, read in order, and from there the raft: a teaching is like a raft you build to cross a river. You don't carry it on your head once you're across.
Then the Long Discourses, and the Buddha's advice in his last rains, when he was ill: be an island to yourselves, a refuge to yourselves, with the teaching as your island.
Then the short books: the Sutta Nipata, the Udana, the Itivuttaka.

teach.h: THE MOTHER AND THE UPRIGHT POT.
teach.b: From the Sutta Nipata, the discourse on loving-kindness: as a mother would protect her only child with her life, so keep a boundless heart toward every living being.
Then the Connected and the Numbered Sayings, and from the Book of Threes: keep the pot upright, so what's poured in stays.
Last, the festival year: full moons, ghosts fed, robes sewn in a day, and the passing between the sal trees. All things end.
There's a Pali word for all of this: buddhavacana, the word of the Buddha. Schools of Buddhism draw the edges of that word differently.
Theravada keeps the Pali canon; Mahayana schools also treasure sutras that year four will open, each in its own terms.
This year stayed with the early discourses. Not the whole forest. A good handful.

how: Many Buddhists study the discourses through chanting, reading groups and Dhamma talks, and in many monasteries and homes a favorite verse or sutta line is recited daily or kept close as a reminder.

o: the word of the Buddha, his teaching
a commentary written about the Buddha
a monk's vow to study every sutta

p: a mother protecting her only child

s: the raft is meant to be carried after you cross
the simile says you leave it at the shore; the teaching is for crossing.
all Buddhist schools draw the edges of the Buddha's word the same way
Theravada keeps the Pali canon; Mahayana schools also treasure later sutras.
the eightfold path begins with view
right view comes first, and concentration closes the list.

games.q: you've built a raft and crossed the river. it served you well. what does the Buddha say to do with it?
o: carry it with you, out of gratitude.
leave it at the shore and go on.
burn it so no one else can use it.
games.why: in the Middle-Length Sayings, the raft is for crossing over, not for holding onto; you leave it and walk on.

practice: Let one line arrive every few breaths: suffering has a cause, and an end; the middle way; the raft is for crossing; be an island to yourself; a boundless heart, like a mother's; keep the pot upright; all things end.
Let each one land, then let it go. If one stays longer than the others, let it; that might be the line for year three.

wordCard.voice: buddhavacana. The Pali and Sanskrit word for 'the word of the Buddha,' what the schools count as his teaching, closing a year spent with the truths, the path, and the early discourses. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit buddhavacana: the word of the Buddha, what the schools count as his teaching.

carryVoice: Your line: you've read his words. Year three begins with a poet. Year two, done.

sources.ref: Mahaparinibbana Sutta, Digha Nikaya 16, II.26 (be an island to yourselves)
Avakujja Sutta, Anguttara Nikaya 3.30 (the upright pot)
